   PLEASE SEND YOUR TEXTFILE!
Text is accepted in any form for
OUTLETTERS: wordprocessor files
(say which),typed or handwritten
letters. However, PLEASE send us
a textfile if possible so your
letter needn't be typed again!
The easiest for us to edit are
Tasword 2 files with the right
margin set at 32 but a textfile
in ANY format is appreciated!

Please state if there should be
parts of your letter you do not
wish published but we always use
our discretion anyway. Letters
may also be edited for clarity
and length... Please ask if you
welcome direct correspondence
from other OUTLET readers and we
will publish your full address.

           Bill Clark
         10 Fell Croft
       DALTON-IN-FURNESS
       Cumbria, LA15 8DD

How do you put a boot block on a
+3 disc,ie, so you can load "*".
Also many routines needed.

Also wanted: thermal paper rolls
for a Timex printer.

Is there a routine that can move
from 128K to 48K during a
program and go back into 128K?

Can you load a a program in 48K
mode and then save it to disc as
the disc drive doesn't work in
48K mode.
                  Bill Clark


From Brian Cavers to Bill Clark

A machine code program to write
a bootstrap sector to the +3
disc is given on pages 204 to
207 of the +3 manual.

You can get a box of 5 thermal
paper rolls for a Timex or
Alphacom printer for `11.95 from
MicroSnips, 25-29 Grange Road
West, Birkenhead, Merseyside,
L41 4BY. (Tel: 051 650 0500).

ROUTE 48 (OUTLET 31) switches
from 128K mode to 48K during a
running program but I have not
been able to find any method of
switching from 48K to 128K with-
out stopping the program. I've
tried for years!


RANDOMIZE USR 23354 will go back
to 128K of course(unless the 48K
printer buffer as used by the
Timex printer has been altered!)
but the program will stop.

I am sure it must be possible
but I don't know how. I'd love
to know myself!

I do have a program that will
access the +3 drive in 48K but
it is copyright and very slow.

                      Brian

From John Cleveland, LONDON

With reference to your reply to
Ron Smith's letter (OUTLET 77),
the +3 printer pokes are:

POKE 23354,62: POKE 23355,16:
POKE 23399,20

It is usually convenient to put
them in a program line in DISK.

Neil Rotherham (OUTLET 76) may
like to know that the +D version
of PCG-DTP (WORDMASTER &c.) is
now available from:

      Format Publications
        34 Bourton Road
      Gloucester, GL4 0LE
        tel: 0452-412572


Alternatively, he might try the
microdrive-compatible cassette
version which provides for
drives 1 and 2 as well as tape
(drive "0").

With the aid of the information
you gave in reply to Geoff
Harris last month, I managed to
convert all the OUTDEX data
files up to issue 76 into MF+3
format and merge them into a
single file which, after erasure
of the duplicate postings in
Issues 65 & 66, consists of 1033
records, the total size being
41K, which leaves 22K of free
RAM space. It would appear that
only the basic data has trans-
ferred and the display formats,
help pages &c. will need to be
reconstructed.

I'm surprised at your reluctance
to provide OUTDEX in MF+3 format
in view of its considerable
advantages, not least amongst
which is having all the data in
one file.

I'm more than a little perturbed
by the almost complete lack of
protection afforded to +3 discs
in recent OUTLET postings. These
discs are not very robust and
I've already had one breakage
which, you may recall, I had to
return for replacement. The mere
sight of one of these flimsy
packets on the doormat gives me
the heebie-jeebies!
               Yours sincerely,

                J.R.Cleveland


Brian Cavers to John Cleveland

My reluctance to provide OUTDEX
in MASTERFILE +3 format is just
because of the extra time needed
to convert it each month.The 48K
version is standard to any mach-
ine and so MUST continue. This
means any +3 version would be an
ADDITIONAL amount of work and of
disc space.Barely a month passes
without the possibility of some
new job. Each one may only be an
hour or so but they all add up
and I am already over-extended.
It is an endless worry to keep
up with the seemingly unlimited
pile of jobs to do each month!
When we are rich and famous and
employ a dozen or so staff then
I may think again!


Sorry about the packaging. I've
passed a copy of your letter to
Ron for consideration of that
point.

We guarantee that a damaged disc
will be replaced by us without
question but I agree that does
not compensate for the inconven-
ience.
                      Brian

Dear Brian & Ron,

The enclosed disc contains a

nal code from Version 09 and
then it only supplies the fields
by numbers after using P(PROMPT/
SEQUENCE).

Brian Cavers to John Lunn


There is no easy way to convert
Tasword +2 for use with +D as
there is with Tasword 2. You
need TASCON +2 from FORMAT. As
you have found out, they do not
normally answer correspondence
even if you are inquiring after
buying something! You need to
either ring their hotline or
just take a chance and order it.

The last time I saw it advert-
ised it was Order code FST-06
and priced `3.95. I'm sure they
still stock it but probably have
not had room to advertise it
recently because of other newer
items.


I was amazed at the problem with
MASTERFILE! Sure enough, your
version of 09 permits entry of
both A to Z AND 0 to 9 but my
own copy (the original BEFORE I
modified it into 09B) does not!

Furthermore, the manual states
quite clearly A-Z. I then went
back to my very first version
from years ago. This turned out
to be Version 08. This too, only
permits entry of A to Z. This is
amazing - it suggests that your
copy was a special modification
either by the author or someone
else to accept 0 to 9.

I had a quick peek through the
code to look for an A to Z test
but could not find one easily.


Suddenly,in a flash,I remembered
a distant memory of some special
POKE at the end of the manual!
Sure enough, a POKE is given to
extend the range. This is what
you do...

Load your MASTERFILE and at the
main menu press U Y U to enter
BASIC. Now enter POKE 65534,48.
Next enter GO TO 1 (do NOT run
as it crashes!). Select V to
SAVE then P to save both the
program and the file (it can be
empty of course).When the option
comes up to "Save Code? (Y/N)"
then press Y to resave the code.

You will find you can now enter
0 to 9 as data references (so
long as you have a file loaded!)


You will also now be able to use
the punctuation signs...

         : ; < = > ? @

          ...as data references!

Your earlier copy must have been
modified at some stage I guess.

                        Brian

Thank you for Issue 77. I shall

SPECFILE is a very popular Spec-
trum database. It has the char-

Sam and +D spreadsheet and

I don't know if it will help
Alan Rutherford, but I've been
doing some experimenting with
OPENTYPE files and the following
allows you to convert your old
Tasword 2 files to Tasword 128
tape files or the +D OPENTYPE
version:

1: Load your Tasword 2 file into
a suitable header reader program
and note the length of the file.
The start should be 32000.

2: Reset your computer and load
the file with a simple LOAD ""
CODE.


3: Enter the following program:

 10 FOR x=32063 TO <end> STEP 64
 20 POKE x,0
 30 NEXT x
 40 POKE <end>,0
 50 STOP

Substitute <end> with the length
of the file plus 32000(so if the
length was 2916, <end>= 34916)


4: This is now a Tasword 128 or
Tasword 3 type file, save with
SAVE"conv.DOC"CODE 32000,<end>


     CONVERTING TO OPENTYPE


1: Load the file to address
32000 as before.


2: Enter the following:

  10 OPEN#4;d1;"newfile1_T" OUT
  20 FOR x=32000 to <end>
  30 PRINT #4;CHR$ PEEK x;
  40 NEXT x
  50 CLOSE #*4

The file in memory will be
converted to an OPENTYPE file,
named "newfile1_T". The _T
suffix is neccessary for the +D
version of Tasword 128 when
scanning a disk for files.
.

From Brian Cavers to all

We've got a couple of nice games
to publish in OUTLET soon which
the author sent as PC emulator
files and which I have now put
on +D as +D snapshots.This means
I can't put them on tape or +3
so I began exploring how snap-
shots are stored...

I didn't solve the problem so if
anyone knows of a snapshot tamer
that can convert them to plain,
simple code that can be put on
tape or +3 disc in the usual way
then please let me know!

However, I found out some bits
of info which may be of interest
to others...


The idea behind all snapshots is
that the state of the registers,
etc. and the address to jump to
are stored somewhere - in the
case of the +D they are in the
directory sector for that file.
This is what they seem to be...

     Byte No.     Register
     --------     --------
      221/2          IY
      223/4          IX
      225/6          DE'
      227/8          BC'
      229/30         HL'
      231/2          AF'
      233/4          DE
      235/6          BC
      237/8          HL
      239/40         Don't know!
      241/2          SP


The 'Byte No.'is the actual byte
postion in the half of the dir-
ectory sector so No.1 is the
first byte and 256 the last, not
0 to 255. If the file is stored
in the second half of a direct-
ory sector then add 256 to those
values. I used SEEK N'PEEK from
OUTLET 45 to examine the direct-
ory sectors.

The A register is presumably
used in the +D routine itself to
start the snapshot and so had to
be left until last. Also, the
address to jump to could not be
stored in a register as they
must all be restored to what the
snapshot program set. So, these
are PUSHed on the stack and then
POPped off at the last second...


This is how the bottom of the
stack is...

             STACK
        ---------------
        address to jump
         to in the code
        ---------------
          AF register
        ---------------
         refresh reg'r?
         flag for IM???
        ---------------
In the +D snapshot starter rout-
ine, the AF register must be
POPped at the last minute and
the final command must be a RET
which forces a jump to the
correct address. I couldn't fig-
ure out what the last two bytes
on the stack are.


You can see SP in the directory
sector at position 241/2 is 6
less than when the snapshot was
taken. Once the bottom 4 bytes
are POPped off by the +D routine
and the final two bytes used to
jump to the address in the prog-
ram then SP will be restored.

If you want to examine the file
sectors then I calculated the
position of the stack bottom,ie,
SP, as....
          (SP - 16384)
          ------------
               510
eg,if this gave 96+remainder 186
it means Track 9, Sector 6 from
the first track and sector of
the file with an offset of 186
into the sector.
                   - Brian.

However, I found out some bits of info which may be of interest to others...

The idea behind all snapshots is that the state of the registers, etc. and the address to jump to are stored somewhere - in the case of the +D they are in the directory sector for that file. This is what they seem to be...

Byte No.     Register

```text
     --------     --------
      221/2          IY
      223/4          IX
      225/6          DE'
      227/8          BC'
      229/30         HL'
      231/2          AF'
      233/4          DE
      235/6          BC
      237/8          HL
```

239/40         Don't know!

```text
      241/2          SP
```

The 'Byte No.'is the actual byte postion in the half of the dir- ectory sector so No.1 is the first byte and 256 the last, not 0 to 255. If the file is stored in the second half of a direct- ory sector then add 256 to those values. I used SEEK N'PEEK from OUTLET 45 to examine the direct- ory sectors.

The A register is presumably used in the +D routine itself to start the snapshot and so had to be left until last. Also, the address to jump to could not be stored in a register as they must all be restored to what the snapshot program set. So, these are PUSHed on the stack and then POPped off at the last second...

This is how the bottom of the stack is...

STACK

```text
        ---------------
```

address to jump to in the code

```text
        ---------------
```

AF register

```text
        ---------------
```

refresh reg'r? flag for IM???

```text
        ---------------
```

In the +D snapshot starter rout- ine, the AF register must be POPped at the last minute and the final command must be a RET which forces a jump to the correct address. I couldn't fig- ure out what the last two bytes on the stack are.

You can see SP in the directory sector at position 241/2 is 6 less than when the snapshot was taken. Once the bottom 4 bytes are POPped off by the +D routine and the final two bytes used to jump to the address in the prog- ram then SP will be restored.

If you want to examine the file sectors then I calculated the position of the stack bottom,ie, SP, as....

```text
          (SP - 16384)

               510
```

Проблему я так и не решил, поэтому если кто-то знает «укротитель снепшотов», способный превратить их в чистый, простой код, который можно записать на ленту или диск +3 обычным способом, пожалуйста, дайте мне знать!

Тем не менее, я выяснил кое-какую информацию, которая может быть интересна остальным...

Идея любых снепшотов заключается в том, что состояние регистров и прочего, а также адрес перехода где-то сохраняются — в случае с +D они лежат в секторе каталога для этого файла. Вот за что они, судя по всему, отвечают...

```text
Номер байта     Регистр
-----------     -------
 221/2            IY
 223/4            IX
 225/6            DE'
 227/8            BC'
 229/30           HL'
 231/2            AF'
 233/4            DE
 235/6            BC
 237/8            HL
 239/40         Не знаю!
 241/2            SP
```

«Номер байта» (Byte No.) — это фактическая позиция байта в половине сектора каталога, то есть № 1 — это первый байт, а 256 — последний, а не от 0 до 255. Если файл хранится во второй половине сектора каталога, просто прибавьте 256 к этим значениям. Для исследования секторов каталога я использовал программу SEEK N'PEEK из OUTLET 45.

Регистр A, по-видимому, используется в самой подпрограмме +D для запуска снапшота, поэтому его восстановление пришлось отложить напоследок. Кроме того, адрес для перехода нельзя было сохранять в регистре, так как все они должны быть восстановлены в точности до значений, заданных снапшотом. Поэтому эти данные заносятся в стек через PUSH, а затем снимаются через POP в самую последнюю секунду...

Вот как выглядит вершина стека...

```text
             STACK
        ---------------
        address to jump
         to in the code
        ---------------
          AF register
        ---------------
         refresh reg'r?
         flag for IM???
        ---------------
```

В подпрограмме запуска снапшота в +D регистр AF, должно быть, снимается с вершины стека в самый последний момент, а финальной командой должен быть RET, который и совершает переход по нужному адресу. Что представляют собой последние два байта в стеке, я так и не смог понять.

Вы можете заметить, что SP в секторе каталога в позиции 241/2 на 6 меньше, чем в момент создания снапшота. Как только нижние 4 байта будут сняты процедурой +D с помощью POP, а последние два байта будут использованы для перехода по адресу в программе, SP восстановится.

Если вы захотите изучить секторы файла, то я рассчитал позицию вершины стека, то есть SP, следующим образом:

```text
          (SP - 16384)
          ------------
               510
```

Например, если в результате получается 96 и остаток 186, это означает Track 9, Sector 6 от начального трека и сектора файла со смещением 186 внутри сектора.
